## Add seven twelve times and you visit everything

Go up seven semitones from C and you land on G. Do it again for D, again for A,
and keep going modulo twelve. You'll touch all twelve pitch classes exactly once
before C comes back round. That's the whole generator: one addition and one
remainder.

The picture people draw of it, twelve names arranged in a ring, is pretty but
secondary. What earns the circle its place in your toolkit is the ordering it
produces, because the ordering puts closely related keys next to each other.
Neighbouring major keys share six of their seven pitch classes. C major and G
major disagree about F versus F-sharp and agree about everything else. G and D
disagree only at C. Adjacency here means "one note apart," which is why the same
ordering also tracks how key signatures grow and where each major key finds its
relative minor, three semitones down.

## Walk the circle and count the overlap

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 92
use_synth :piano

define :major_pitch_classes do |root|
  [0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11].map { |offset| (root + offset) % 12 }
end

circle = 12.times.map { |index| (index * 7) % 12 }
names = [:c, :g, :d, :a, :e, :b, :fs, :cs, :gs, :ds, :as, :f]

circle.each_with_index do |pitch_class, index|
  next_class = circle[(index + 1) % circle.length]
  shared = major_pitch_classes(pitch_class) & major_pitch_classes(next_class)
  relative_minor = (pitch_class - 3) % 12
  puts "#{names[index]} pc=#{pitch_class} relative_minor=#{relative_minor} shared=#{shared.length}"

  # values_at(0, 2, 4) picks degrees 1, 3 and 5. first(3) would give you
  # degrees 1, 2 and 3, which is a cluster, not a triad.
  triad = major_pitch_classes(pitch_class).values_at(0, 2, 4)
  play_chord triad.map { |pc| pc + 60 }, release: 0.65, amp: 0.7
  sleep 1
end
```

Twelve lines of log, twelve triads, one long return to C. Read the
`shared=` column first. It reports six every single time, and that constancy is
the structural claim of the lesson sitting in a single integer.

The triads will sound like they keep rearranging themselves, and they do. These
are pitch classes, so anything crossing B wraps back down below the root, and G
major arrives as D-G-B. The chord is right and the voicing is an accident of the
modulo. [Lesson 27](../06-chords-and-harmony/27-inversions-voicing.qmd) is where voicing stops being an accident.

Now look at the `names` array beside the numbers. Pitch class 6 appears as
`:fs`, though nothing in the arithmetic chose that over G-flat. Which spelling
is correct there? Hold the question while you listen to the chords go round; the
integers won't help you with it, and the second half of this lesson is about
why.

## Change the generator

1. Change `7` to `5`. Five semitones up is a perfect fourth, and the walk runs
   the circle backwards through the same twelve pitch classes. Compare the
   printed order against the original before you listen for anything.
2. Print the set difference alongside the intersection. Each clockwise move
   drops degree 4 of the old key and adds the new key's leading tone. Play those
   two notes on their own before each fragment, so the six-note overlap stops
   masking the one decisive change.
3. Drop the rendered fragments an octave. Not a single pitch class or adjacency
   count moves, and the cycle gains considerable weight. Structure and voicing
   are separate questions, and this variation keeps them that way.

## Why seven and twelve get along

Seven and twelve share no factor greater than one, so repeatedly adding seven
modulo twelve reaches every residue before it repeats. Coprimality is doing all
the work. Pick a step that shares a factor with twelve and the cycle closes
early: add six and your generator bounces between two pitch classes forever, add
four and you get three, add three and you get four. Try `(index * 8) % 12` if
you want to watch a circle collapse into a triangle in the log.

So the completeness of the circle isn't a fact about fifths. It's a fact about
the relationship between the step size and the size of the space, and the fifth
happens to be the interval that satisfies it while also sounding stable.

Five satisfies it too, which is what variation 1 demonstrates, and that isn't a
coincidence either: seven and five add to twelve, so the fourth is the fifth
walked the other way. Every circle of fifths you've ever seen is also a circle
of fourths read anticlockwise. One diagram, two generators, depending on which
direction your music is travelling.

## Six notes in common is the whole story

The scale is generated too, and by the same arithmetic. Transpose
`[0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11]` up by seven, reduce modulo twelve, and precisely one
member of the set changes. That single-element difference is what makes
neighbouring keys such a comfortable route for modulation: a piece moving from C
to G keeps six of its seven notes and negotiates only one.

Follow the same move around the circle and you generate the order of sharps for
free. Each clockwise step raises the note that was degree 4 of the old key, and
that raised note becomes the new key's leading tone. F-sharp, then C-sharp, then
G-sharp. Nobody needs to memorise the sequence; it falls out of the addition.

Relative minor is another one-line transformation, `(root - 3) % 12`. A relative
major and minor hold the same seven pitch classes and the same key signature,
and they differ in which note the music treats as home. You've already heard
what that difference does, back in [Lesson 22](22-scale-degrees-pull-toward-home.qmd), when swapping a C drone for A
turned the same melody inside out.

## Where integers stop being enough

Pitch class 6 is pitch class 6. Your speakers can't tell you whether it's
F-sharp or G-flat, and neither can the modulo arithmetic, but the distinction is
real: F-sharp major and G-flat major have different key signatures, different
staff spellings, and different implications for what comes next. That's why the
program carries a parallel `names` array. As in [Lesson 10](../02-pitch-space/10-sharps-flats-why-spelling-sound.qmd), the moment two
identical numbers need different written names, your data model needs a named
field to hold the difference.

The playback here renders something deliberately rough. It takes the first three
sorted pitch classes and lifts them into one register, which is not reliably a
root-position triad, because a modular set has already thrown away octave order.
Build a harmonic renderer properly and you'd regenerate the scale above its
actual root, then select degrees 1, 3 and 5. The crude voicing survives in this
lesson because it keeps your attention on intersection and adjacency, which are
the structures the example exists to expose.

Part 6 picks the voicing question back up and makes it the subject. Once you
stack thirds into triads, the difference between a chord's pitch classes and a
chord's actual arrangement in register stops being a technicality and starts
being the sound.

## Build the key record

Write `key_record(index)` covering circle positions `-7` through `7`. Each
record holds the tonic spelling, the accidental count and type, the
relative-minor spelling, and the two neighbouring keys. Derive every field from
the position; don't transcribe a fifteen-row table out of a textbook.

Print the whole run from seven flats to seven sharps, then play each tonic triad
in that order. When a printed spelling and a played chord seem to disagree,
suspect the representation before you touch the synth. Nine times in ten the
arithmetic is right and the spelling policy is what needs a decision.
